note:
A DE moment is a point at which the direction should change. The practitioner named it on 2026-10-15, after finding that a map still had an Input mode a day after the discussion that ruled against modes: "The map output discussion is what we call a DE moment, a moment when things should head in a different direction, and it did not."

This file is the answer to that. Every direction a discussion settles is recorded here with what it requires IN CODE and a clock on it, because the failure mode is specific and this project has produced it at least three times: the direction is written into a spec page, a glossary entry or an ontology term, the code is left alone, and the record now says the matter is settled while the running application still does the old thing. A widget page is not a work item and no ratchet can see one.

It is deliberately not the blocker ledger. A blocker is a claim that something CANNOT be done yet. A direction is a decision that something SHOULD now be done differently, and the two fail in opposite ways: a blocker rots by being lifted and not noticed, a direction rots by being agreed and not built.
windowBasis: The same window the blocker ledger uses, for the same reason: this project changes in days. A direction nobody has checked in a week is a direction nobody is acting on, and saying so is the entire point of the file.

The file-level count that made this look like 83 files of work was wrong: widgets/blockers.json holds 21 uses and only the single STANDING entry was live, the other three being lifted, narrowed and withdrawn entries that are records. docs/audits/ontology-audit.md holds 16 and 14 are inside the dated section that withdrew the term. directions.statedBy: the practitioner, in the 65 amendment and experiment 106
directions.inTheirWords: In a nutshell, a ruleset widget is like a mini-software program with many possibilities because of how rules may be combined to produce an output. — and, on 2026-10-15, looking at the shipped Inspector: "Regarding ruleset widgets, this is not the design we discussed, the rules are pinned not very flexible."
directions.requiresInCode: The authored form of 106 -- condition {field, comparator, value}, AND groups, OR of groups, a LIST of conclusions from the declared output vocabulary -- with a total compiler to the N3 subset 65 settled, a rule-count ceiling checkable from the form before compiling, and the Inspector authoring rules rather than choosing a pre-baked ruleset from a list of four.
directions.workItem: 106, whose closing condition is Group A green and B1 green against the three existing rulesets on their frozen fixtures

checks.found: Nothing of it is built. No comparator, no authored form, no compiler in src/rulesets.ts or src/rule-application.ts; 106 has been `asked` since 2026-10-12. What shipped is the OTHER half of 65 -- rules as declared versioned data, one widget hosting them, three widgets retired -- which is real and is not this. The practitioner meets a dropdown of four bundled rulesets whose rule text is fixed, and the only thing they can change is a declared parameter such as a 5 km threshold. "The rules are pinned" is exactly accurate. 106 says what must come first and it needs no new oracle: B1, the three existing rulesets rebuilt in the authored form and compiled, reaching identical conclusions on their frozen fixtures.

Acted on, partly, the same day. The authored form and its compiler are built in src/authored-rules.ts and B1 is GREEN: all three shipped rulesets rebuilt in the form, compiled, and reasoned under the real EYE engine reach identical conclusions. A1, A2, A3, A5, A8, A9 and A10 pass too, and the rule ceiling is checked from the form before anything is compiled. 106 moves asked -> tried. What is NOT built is the half the practitioner meets: the Inspector still offers a ruleset chosen from a list, so the rules are still pinned from where they sit. Four comparators compile and have never been executed, so by 106's own rule they must not be offered until B2 passes.

Carried further the same day, on the practitioner's proposal: "We should have a worked example just for the ruleset widget to exercise different ruleset conditions so users can also see examples of how to configure it. That is one way to execute widget rules and validate at the same time." Built as the `rulesets` workspace: three steps, one condition kind each -- a band from two comparisons, alternatives with two conclusions at once, a category match -- over twelve synthetic records chosen so every branch has one. A node can now CARRY authored rules and a generic path runs them: facts from declared field bindings, the authored form compiled, conclusions back onto the records. Two things the example found that no unit test would: the Inspector described the PINNED ruleset, so a step applying authored rules showed somebody else's title, threshold and basis; and authored rules MINT VOCABULARY -- thirty terms in one afternoon -- which now lives in urn:fieldwork:authored: so a practitioner's coinage is never mistaken for a term this application defines. The Inspector reads the rules back in plain words. What is still missing is composing them there: the rules can be read and their numbers changed, not yet written.

Built. The practitioner opened the published example -- "I see the ruleset widget but it's not editable" -- and then chose the shape: "Perhaps the rule editor should be a modal dialog so there is enough space." src/rule-editor.ts edits 106's authored form in a dialog: conditions grouped by and, alternatives by or, a list of conclusions, add and remove throughout. The compiler runs on every edit, so the rule ceiling and any refusal appear while authoring rather than at the end, and Keep is disabled while the rules cannot compile. Comparators are filtered by the field's kind, so a category cannot be given `is more than`, and the fwa: namespace is added for the practitioner rather than typed by them. Three debts recorded in 106 rather than hidden: two comparators are offered that have never been executed against the real engine, nothing catches an incommensurable unit at authoring time, and conclusions are free text so two rules can disagree -- caught at run time, which is late.

directions.statedBy: the practitioner, reading the network_input manual page
directions.inTheirWords: Regarding street network, OSMNx designates a download as walk or drive. I noticed in the widget manual that it talks about walk but it could be drive. Do we make that distinction when we download an OSM street network? — and, settling the scope: "For 1854 Soho, driving speed limits does not matter. For current day investigations, these speed limits matter as a ceiling (best case travel time)."
directions.requiresInCode: A travelMode chosen on `network_input` at download time, which selects the highway list (driving adds motorway, trunk and their links and drops footway, path, steps, pedestrian and cycleway), the restriction tags read (motor_vehicle, motorcar and access rather than foot and oneway:foot) and the direction tag that makes an edge one-way. The graph records its mode in `source` and in the download receipt, and a downstream widget whose `travelMode` disagrees with the graph's mode refuses rather than computes.
directions.workItem: 126, whose first half is the mode; the bound semantics are the second half and are a separate direction

checks.found: Nothing of it is built, and the gap is wider than the manual page. `WALKABLE_HIGHWAYS` in src/street-network.ts is one list used twice -- in the Overpass query and again in networkFromOSM -- and it excludes motorway, trunk and their links entirely, so a driving network is not merely unfiltered here, it is missing the roads that carry cars. Restrictions read are foot ones (foot=no|private|use_sidepath, barrier nodes, oneway:foot), and the source string says outright that vehicle oneway does not imply foot oneway. Meanwhile `reachable_nodes` ALREADY takes travelMode walking|cycling|driving|other with per-mode speed bands that refuse an implausible speed, and the Inspector offers it as "How people travel" -- so the mode is declared where it cannot be honoured and absent where it would be. Measured on examples/john-snow/soho.graphml, the OSMnx walk graph this repository ships: of 1,619 directed edges and 50.63 km, 918 edges and 24.34 km (56.7% of edges, 48.1% of length) are types OSMnx's drive filter excludes, and 455 edges (28.1%) carry oneway=True whose direction we ignore because we read oneway:foot only. A driving isochrone on that graph routes over footways, up steps, and the wrong way down a quarter of the one-way streets. Not established: how wrong the resulting time is, which is unmeasured; Soho is half a square kilometre of dense centre so the shares elsewhere will differ; and OSMnx's drive filter is one project's definition, not a standard.

Built the same day, on the practitioner's go-ahead: "So before I download Bunia again, I want to be able to set driving mode on the street network." MODE_FILTERS in src/street-network.ts is one table with a row per difference -- highway list, the access tags consulted, the values that forbid and permit, the one-way tag, whether a roundabout implies direction, and the sentence saved on the graph -- so the two modes cannot drift into two parsers. Driving follows OSMnx's drive exclusions so the two implementations stay comparable, and keeps `road`, as OSMnx does. The mode is in the query text, which is the cache key, so a driving download cannot be served a cached walking graph; it is written into provenance, shown on the widget, and asserted as fw:travelMode on the network entity rather than only inside the metadata blob. refuseModeMismatch in src/reachable-nodes.ts refuses a declared mode the graph cannot carry and names the way out, but only a KNOWN contradiction: an imported file carries no mode, and cycling or `other` have no download of their own, so neither is locked out. Walking is the default, so a saved workflow downloads what it always did. Ten unit tests in tests/street-network-mode.test.mjs and one browser test for the control. One list claim I had to correct against the data: nine of the fifteen walkable highway values are also drivable, so the LISTS mostly agree -- it is the edges that diverge, 56.7% of them on the Soho graph. network_input 0.3.0, manual page rewritten with a comparison table, CHANGELOG under 0.10.0. What is NOT built: the graph carries no speed limits, no junction delay and no congestion, so a driving travel time is one speed over every street, which is the subject of the other direction and of 126.

directions.statedBy: the practitioner, on whether OSM carries speed limits
directions.inTheirWords: For 1854 Soho, driving speed limits does not matter. For current day investigations, these speed limits matter as a ceiling (best case travel time). Worst case travel time can be researched. — and, on where the obligation falls: "Do not worry about the local trip time license, that is the user's problem, the thing to worry about is if it is recorded in the widget, a provenance note goes with it for the benefit of accurate reporting, for example during publications."
directions.requiresInCode: Any travel time derived from a per-edge posted limit is reported as a BOUND and named as one -- in the result field, in the N3 receipt and in the Inspector -- rather than as an estimate, with the edges that had no limit and fell back to a declared speed counted in both. A widget that can produce only a best case refuses the claim a best case cannot support: a free-flow time can rule a site out of a catchment and cannot rule one in, so "not reachable even at best" is sound and "reachable" is not. And a speed or trip time a practitioner supplies carries a PROVENANCE NOTE that travels with it into the receipt, the evidence panel and any export, so a figure quoted in a publication can be attributed. Not a licence check: whose data it is remains the practitioner's to answer. This applies to the single speedMPerMin that already exists and carries no note today, not only to a future per-edge speed.
directions.workItem: 126, whose closing condition is a bound named in the result and the receipt, plus best and worst computed over one current-day graph and differing by a measured amount

checks.found: Nothing to label yet, because no widget reads a posted limit: `maxspeed` appears nowhere in src/, docs/ or scripts/, although the Overpass query asks for way tags and the tag arrives in the response and is dropped. Travel time is one scalar everywhere -- minutes x speedMPerMin over every edge identically -- and src/reachable-nodes.ts already says so in the receipt it writes, which is the honest version of the current model and not the thing this direction changes. What this direction adds to the earlier framing, and what 126 records, is the asymmetry: an access claim is conservative in the WORST case, so coverage computed from a ceiling overstates access, invisibly, because the output is a number of minutes like any other. Measured on examples/john-snow/soho.graphml: 499 of 1,619 edges carry maxspeed (30.8%), or 469 of 701 drive-usable edges (66.9%) and 17.54 of 26.29 km (66.7%), with values `30 mph` and `20 mph` -- free text with units, where the wider database legally holds 50, RU:urban, walk, none and signals. So a third of the drivable length in a well-mapped city centre needs a declared fallback. Not established: that posted limits would make a driving time more accurate, which is unmeasured against any observed trip, and that 66.9% generalises -- it is one half-square-kilometre graph read from a file we ship.

Scope corrected the same day, before anything was built on the earlier reading. 126 had made the licence of a worst-case speed source a question for this project to settle; it is not. What is: every configurable speed in the application today -- isochrone's speedMPerMin, reachable_nodes', travel_time's, access' -- is a bare number with no note of where it came from, so in a receipt it is indistinguishable from a figure this application derived. That is the gap to close, and it is open now rather than when per-edge speeds arrive.

directions.inTheirWords: I created a dive-deeper repo on GitHub so the dive deeper notebooks do not mix with the validation lab's. — and, when nothing had changed in the code a day later: "are we using the dive deeper repo for the dive deeper pedagogy notebooks?"

The application links the new site for a widget that has a lesson; scripts/validate-dive-deeper.mjs verifies lesson notebooks against ../dive-deeper/content and refuses a lesson no widget links; and the sections still living inside lab notebooks are counted against a ceiling that may fall and never rise.
directions.workItem: 94, whose closing condition is whether the notebook is the right surface at all

checks.found: Recorded and not built, which is the failure this ledger exists to catch. The split was written into experiment 94 with its costs and its ratchet, and the code still read ../validation-lab/content, linked the Lab's site, and carried `diveDeeper` as a heading inside a parity notebook. The repository had been created that morning and was EMPTY. I had not even recorded it here, so no clock was running on it; four defect reports came in and it went unlooked-at until the practitioner asked.

Built the same day. digital-twin-ph/dive-deeper is seeded: README stating what a notebook owes, Apache-2.0, JupyterLite config pinned to the Lab's builder versions, a Pages workflow that executes every notebook before publishing, and the first lesson -- the mean centre on Snow's 250 addresses. It meets the pedagogical requirements rather than the older narrower definition, and its three measured numbers are the lesson: weighting by deaths moves the centre 2.10 m, mean against median centre 6.62 m, UTM 30N against British National Grid 0.001 m. So the weighting a practitioner reaches for first matters least -- a weighted mean only moves when the weights are spatially structured, which the notebook then shows by weighting eastward and moving it 46 m -- and the summary nobody questions matters most, the mean centre having a breakdown point of zero. In Fieldwork: widgets/dive-deeper.json pins the repo at 04b22ab, the validator checks lessons against ../dive-deeper/content and holds the legacy count at 20, and the Inspector links the new site. What is NOT done: twenty sections remain inside lab notebooks, and rewriting one is new work rather than a file move.

directions.workItem: 122, whose phase two is sharing data between a project's workflows

directions.statedBy: the practitioner, on the handle limit built an hour earlier
directions.inTheirWords: If it's a jurisdictional polygon as a study area, I don't think we should make the vertices draggable. That would be changing the shape, provenance and authoritativeness of the polygon.
directions.requiresInCode: The study-area dialog offers no vertex handles for a geometry that carries an acquisition record, whatever its size, and says why rather than silently omitting them. The provenance machinery is unchanged: a boundary modified by any other route still names its source and records fw:geometryAsPublished false, because a shape that was edited and says nothing is worse than one that was edited and says so.
directions.workItem: the study-area widget's own checklist pass, where the drawing surface is reviewed

checks.found: Built, and it corrected a fix made an hour earlier for a different reason. Profiling had shown that one draggable Leaflet marker per vertex was what froze the dialog on North Kivu's 16,548 vertices and killed WebKit, so handles were capped at 400 -- which answered the PERFORMANCE question and got the principle wrong: a district of 40 vertices sits far below any cap and would still have offered the gesture. The question is not how many vertices there are, it is whose shape it is. Handles are now refused for any geometry carrying an acquisition record, with a line saying the outline is a published jurisdiction and that drawing your own shape is the way to a different area. The 400 limit stays beneath it for a large geometry that arrived some other way, since nobody draws four hundred vertices by hand. Pinned by a test on a 40-vertex unit, so it measures the principle and not the size.

directions.statedBy: the practitioner, on finding 526 of 961 facilities outside the study area
directions.inTheirWords: We do not have a point in polygon process. — and, when shown pointRelation in spatial-predicates.ts: "I mean widget." — and, on what it should show: "clip_points_to_area can have a knob that shows which points are outside but still exclude them in the output."
directions.requiresInCode: A primitive that takes an area and a point layer and outputs the points inside it, with its own node on the canvas and its own receipt naming the OGC predicate, whether boundary points were kept, and the three counts. The predicate itself is not rewritten: pointRelation already decides this for catchments, the map, input data, the raster mask and the coverage check, and a sixth implementation would be the copy this project keeps finding.
directions.workItem: 64, the widget budget, which this moves away from on purpose and which has to be told why

checks.found: Built as clip_points_to_area. The gap was precise: eleven widgets emit a point layer and none of them answered 'keep the ones inside this area'. coverage_check REPORTS membership and outputs a review, summarize_points_to_polygon COUNTS it, a map draws the split -- so the decision could be read and could not be made, except privately inside whatever widget needed it, which is how it came to be buried in a source widget with no node and no receipt. A point ON the outline is kept by default and the choice is a parameter, because strict containment is what sfWithin means and the two give different counts on exactly the data where it matters. I had also hand-rolled ray casting in facility-records.ts an hour earlier, a sixth implementation that threw away the Boundary relation; it now calls pointRelation like everything else. The widget costs the budget: 47 live against a target of 41, six away rather than five, and experiment 64 is told so rather than left to notice.

Carried further the same day on the practitioner's shape for it. The widget now keeps the features it set aside and offers them for DRAWING while passing on only what is in the area: a connected map adds them as rows in the Outside colour it already has, marked so nothing reads them as records the workflow holds. The reason is the one the practitioner gave by sending a picture rather than a number -- 526 facilities in a tight cluster over one border is a different fact from 526 scattered in every direction, and the count 526 does not distinguish them. Default on. A record with no coordinates is counted as set aside and is NOT offered for drawing, because there is nowhere to draw it.

directions.inTheirWords: But a study area is a polygon.
directions.requiresInCode: The `area` and `polygons` port types stop being two unrelated things. An area carries a Boundary -- a Polygon or MultiPolygon -- and Combined area ('Overlapping and touching areas become one') refuses it because its port says `polygons`. Either the union takes areas and returns an area, or an area is readable wherever a polygon is. What must not stand is a widget that does exactly what the practitioner asked for, one port type away from the thing they have.

checks.found: Stated on being told that two adjacent study areas cannot be merged after the fact. They can be merged AT ACQUISITION -- the boundary picker takes several units at one level and builds a MultiPolygon with provenance naming each -- but the Combined area widget, whose whole description is 'overlapping and touching areas become one', takes a polygons result and so cannot be fed a study area. The distinction between the two types is this application's, not the domain's: an area is a boundary with provenance, a Polygons is features with a method, and a study area is a polygon in both readings. Nothing built.

directions.inTheirWords: Is that another cap?
directions.requiresInCode: The caps ledger watches four files and the application holds fifty-two exported numeric constants across twenty-five. Twenty-six of them are invisible to the ratchet, among them MAX_RASTER_CELLS, which refuses a raster window rather than a drawing and so decides how much of a study area may be analysed at all; also REPROJECT_MAX_RECORDS, RULE_CEILING, MAX_PDF_BYTES, ISOCHRONE_TIMEOUT_MS and OSM_PAUSE_MAX_MS. Watching every file is necessary and not sufficient: scripts/validate-caps.mjs matches `export const NAME=<number>`, so the refusal at project-files.ts on `blockWidth*blockHeight*bytesPerPixel > 64_000_000` escapes by being an inline literal with no name. The ledger must cover every file, and the check must reach comparisons against literals, or declaring a cap stays optional and the rule is therefore optional too.
directions.workItem: Add the remaining twenty-one files to widgets/caps.json watchedFiles and declare what that surfaces; then extend the validator past named constants to the literals a refusal compares against. The ledger was built while chasing the street network widget and has the scope of that chase: twenty-six caps, four files, one subsystem. The practitioner met MAX_RASTER_CELLS the way they met attempt-seconds -- by being refused -- which is the thing the ledger exists to prevent.

directions.inTheirWords: It's the approach we decided to pursue with that other project -- Epi Info AI -- in designing the GIS kernel.
directions.requiresInCode: A street graph is held as JavaScript objects with string identifiers: roughly 100 to 200 bytes a junction against about 24 for a packed struct, and a garbage collector that turns building one into a superlinear cost -- measured 2026-10-22 in a Chromium tab at 324 ms for 100,000 junctions, 4.4 s for 500,000 and 20.9 s for a million. The same day a province arrived as 200 MB of Overpass JSON that had to become one JavaScript string to be parsed, which is where V8 refuses with "Invalid string length", and the project export meets the same ceiling from the other side. The Rust street engine already reads a 416 MB .osm.pbf and clips it to a polygon during decode, at a scale the TypeScript download path does not reach: the experiment has been run and the kernel won it. What it does not yet own is the graph. Overpass responses should be parsed in wasm, nodes and edges held in linear memory, and TypeScript given typed-array views for drawing and routing -- the shape Epi Info AI settled on for its Epi kernel, where Rust owns the deterministic primitives and the host owns the surfaces.
directions.workItem: Fieldwork already carries what the Epi kernel design depends on: a Rust/WASM kernel in vendor/street-engine.wasm, a parity ledger and validation lab for parity-tested primitives, and since 2026-10-22 a caps ledger whose budgets are measured rather than chosen. The piece missing is ownership of the graph. Worth scoping against what it would NOT fix, which is most of what cost days: a borrowed 180-second clock, an undeclared MAX_RASTER_CELLS, a 20 MB import limit, Geofabrik links nobody could find and a project export behind a storage readout. A kernel raises the ceiling; it does not make a number measured or a door visible.
